market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: Which plant milk has the least sugar and fewest calories?

seo.title: Lowest-sugar, lowest-calorie plant milks compared
seo.meta_description: Unsweetened almond, oat and soy milks can differ sharply in calories and protein. Compare current U.S. labels and see why lowest calorie is not the whole story.
seo.search_intent: Find the plant milk lowest in sugar and calories

excerpt: There is no permanent category winner because formulas change, but current U.S. examples show the trade-off clearly: Silk Unsweet Almondmilk has 30 calories and 0 g sugar per cup, Oatly Unsweetened Oatmilk has 40 calories per cup, and Silk Unsweet Soymilk has 80 calories but 8 g protein and less than 1 g sugar. Lowest calorie and most nutritionally similar to milk are different questions.
content_html:
If you only ask which plant milk is lowest in calories, unsweetened almond milk often wins. But the lightest product is not automatically the closest nutritional replacement for dairy milk.

Three current U.S. examples

Per 1 cup (240 mL)Unsweet almondUnsweet oatUnsweet soy
Calories304080
Total sugars0 gCheck current label<1 g
Protein1 gVaries by formula8 g

The almond example is lowest in calories, while soy provides eight times as much protein as that almond milk.

Unsweetened matters more than the plant name

Original, vanilla and barista versions may add sugar or more oil. Two oat milks from the same brand can differ by more than 100 calories per cup. Oatly currently lists 40 calories for Unsweetened and 160 for Full Fat.

Zero sugar does not mean complete nutrition

Silk Unsweet Almondmilk has 0 g sugar and 30 calories, but only 1 g protein. Silk Unsweet Soymilk has less than 1 g sugar and 80 calories but 8 g protein, plus calcium and vitamin D fortification.

What the FDA recommends checking

The FDA advises comparing protein, calcium, vitamin D and potassium as well as added sugars and saturated fat. Fortified soy beverage is the plant alternative currently treated as nutritionally similar enough to milk to sit in the Dairy Group of U.S. dietary guidance.

The lightest drink is not always the most useful replacement

Unsweetened almond, coconut, and cashew beverages often appear among the lowest-calorie options, but many provide very little protein. Unsweetened soy milk may contain somewhat more energy while supplying far more protein and often coming closer to dairy milk nutritionally. If a plant beverage routinely replaces milk rather than appearing only as a splash in coffee, that tradeoff can matter more than saving a few dozen calories per cup.

“No added sugar” and “zero sugar” also require label reading. Some products contain carbohydrate naturally from the base ingredient even without added sweeteners. Manufacturing processes can also break starch into smaller sugars, changing total sugar without table sugar appearing in the ingredient list. Comparing both total sugars and added sugars gives a clearer picture.

Fortification varies widely. Calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12 are not present in equivalent amounts across all plant beverages, and added minerals can settle during storage. Shaking the carton before pouring helps redistribute them. For young children, pregnancy, food allergies, or highly restricted diets, choosing a milk substitute should consider specific nutrient needs rather than calories alone.

Serving context changes the importance of the numbers. A tablespoon in coffee contributes little regardless of the brand, whereas an 8- to 12-ounce breakfast serving magnifies the difference between products. A useful choice balances calories and sugar with protein, fortification, ingredient preferences, and a taste you will actually use consistently.

Packaging format can make comparisons look more dramatic than they are. U.S. Nutrition Facts panels commonly use a cup-sized serving, while other markets often list values per 100 milliliters. Convert products to the same volume before ranking them. A carton that appears lower in sugar or calories may simply be using a smaller labeled serving.

Sweetened vanilla, chocolate, barista, and flavored versions should be treated as separate products rather than as representatives of the base plant. A brand's unsweetened almond milk and its barista almond beverage can differ substantially in oil, carbohydrate, and calories even though both say “almond” on the front.

Culinary performance is another reason not to rank plant milks on calories alone. Protein and fat affect foaming, emulsification, and body. A very light almond beverage may behave differently in coffee or sauce from soy milk, while “barista” versions are often formulated with extra fat or stabilizers for texture. The lowest-calorie carton may therefore be a poor functional substitute in a recipe even if it wins a nutrition-table comparison.

People who use plant milk mainly for coffee can prioritize taste and added sugar because the portion is small. Someone drinking several cups daily should pay much more attention to protein, fortification, and total intake. The same product can be a minor flavoring in one diet and a major nutrient source in another.

Bottom line

For the fewest calories among these examples, unsweet almond wins. For a higher-protein milk replacement, unsweet soy is much closer to dairy milk. Choose the actual carton, not the category stereotype.

faq.question: Which plant milk has the fewest calories?
faq.answer: Among the current examples here, Silk Unsweet Almondmilk at 30 calories per cup, versus 40 for Oatly Unsweetened and 80 for Silk Unsweet Soymilk.

faq.question: Which has the least sugar?
faq.answer: Silk Unsweet Almondmilk lists 0 g total sugar; Silk Unsweet Soymilk lists less than 1 g and 0 g added sugar.

faq.question: Is almond milk better because it has fewer calories?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. It has much less protein than soy in these examples: 1 g versus 8 g per cup.

faq.question: What should I check besides sugar?
faq.answer: Protein, calcium, vitamin D, potassium, saturated fat and whether the product is fortified.
